_reference.source: MEASURED from Apple's official iOS and iPadOS 27 UI Kit for Figma (community file 1651309003795292092, kit version 27.0.2, 2026-07-16) via the Figma REST API on 2026-07-29. Supplemented by the WWDC 2026 keynote and Platforms State of the Union (2026-06-08).
_reference.note: Values tagged _measured come from the kit's own layers. Apple publishes no numeric spec for the Liquid Glass material itself — the kit approximates it in Figma, and this file transcribes that approximation for the web. On Apple platforms use the SwiftUI glassEffect API.
_reference._assetPolicy: Measurements are documented here; Apple's kit file, artwork, and vector data are not redistributed.
_reference._figmaGlassEffect: The kit's glass surfaces carry a Figma GLASS effect whose parameters the REST API does not expose. What IS exposed — fills, drop shadows, inner shadows, background blurs, corner radii — is captured below. The CSS reproduction is therefore close but not identical.
_reference._kitIsAnApproximation: The kit reproduces Liquid Glass in Figma for design work. Whether its construction — the spread-shadow ring plus two offset inner shadows — matches how the system actually composites the material at runtime is unverified. Treat these as the kit's values, which is what a designer hands you, not as the system's internal parameters.

transparency._description: iOS 27 replaces the binary Reduce Transparency toggle with a system-wide slider running from ultra clear to fully tinted. Apps inherit the resulting appearance; there is no per-app override. On the web, model it as one custom property that scales glass opacity and blur together.
transparency._semantics: 0 = fully tinted (opaque, closest to pre-Liquid-Glass chrome). 1 = ultra clear (maximum see-through).

fullyTinted.note: Opaque chrome. Nearest equivalent to the iOS 26 Reduce Transparency look, without the flattening.

default.note: System default. Already more diffused than the iOS 26 default.

ultraClear.note: Maximum transparency. Verify foreground contrast per surface.

transparency._accessibility: Accessibility wins, and Apple documents this: per the iPhone user guide, if Reduce Transparency or Increase Contrast is on, you must turn it off before the Liquid Glass appearance can be changed. The web reproduction matches — every preset selector is repeated inside the prefers-reduced-transparency block at equal specificity but later in source order, so the accessibility value wins even when a preset class sits on the element.

_derive._description: The two scale factors are derived from the slider value in CSS so --ios27-glass-transparency is the single source of truth. NOT measured — the slider is a runtime system setting with no kit representation, so this curve is a web-side model. Validated against the native material: at t=0.5 it yields alpha 0.735 for regular glass, and a SwiftUI .glassEffect(.regular) screenshot over known colours on iOS 26.5 solves to 0.729 as a channel mean (0.8% off).

transparency._location: Settings > Appearance > Liquid Glass. A continuous slider with a live preview. It supersedes the Clear / Tinted selector that iOS 26.1 put under Display & Brightness > Liquid Glass.
transparency._appApi: No public API or SwiftUI environment value for reading the slider is documented. Apps using system materials inherit the appearance. Do not assume a readable value exists.

liquidGlass._disclaimer: Numeric values (opacity/blur/frost/depth/splay/shadow/edge/specular) APPROXIMATE the native material for web/CSS rendering. Apple publishes no numeric values for the Liquid Glass material.
liquidGlass._placement: Liquid Glass is a floating navigation/controls layer ABOVE content. Use for toolbars, tab bars, floating controls, sheet chrome. Do NOT apply to content backgrounds, large areas, or stack glass on glass.

_variants.clear: More transparent — ONLY over media-rich/colorful content with a high-contrast foreground.
_variants.identity: No glass (conditional disable without layout change), e.g. glassEffect(isEnabled ? .regular : .identity).

_ios27Changes: Kit change log 27.0.0: updated appearance of all liquid glass components; updated soft and hard Scroll Edge Effects; the 'State' property of Liquid Glass - Regular became a boolean named 'Prominent'.
Existing apps inherit the material changes on iOS 27 without recompiling.

regular._measured: Liquid Glass - Regular - Large / Medium / Small in the kit.
regular._note: Large and Medium measured identical in 27.0.2 — same fills, shadows, and 34pt radius. They differ only by usage context.

small._states: Measured axes: Mode x Active x Prominent.

prominent._description: Active + Prominent adds an opaque white backing plus a tint layer composited with LINEAR_BURN.
prominent._api: There is NO Glass.prominent variant in SwiftUI. Glass exposes regular / clear / identity. What the kit calls Prominent corresponds to the .glassProminent button style, which has existed since iOS 26.0 — it is not new in iOS 27. What changed in 27 is the kit property: Liquid Glass - Regular's "State" became a boolean named "Prominent".

clear._measured: Liquid Glass - Clear in the kit.
clear._usage: Only over media-rich or colorful content; add a scrim if legibility is at risk.

rim._description: The outline around a glass surface. Measured as zero-blur DROP_SHADOWs with positive spread — a light grey ring, NOT the dark inset border previously assumed here.

innerShadow._description: Top and bottom inner shadows on the Glass Effect layer. This is what reads as the lit rim on device — implemented as dark inner shadows offset beyond the shape, not as a white highlight.
innerShadow._note: Applied twice, at +40 and -40 on Y.

smallExtra._note: Small glass adds a third, lighter inner shadow from below.

_swiftuiApi._note: Prominence is expressed through component styles and roles, not through a material variant.

backgroundMaterials._measured: _Materials/Mode Options component set in the kit. Light and Dark measured separately; the IC-Light / IC-Dark variants measured identical to their non-IC counterparts, consistent with increased contrast being retired as an authoring mode.
backgroundMaterials._note: Light materials are white-based, dark materials are black-based. Rendering the light values on a dark page produces a conspicuous light panel — always emit both.

scrollEdgeEffect._measured: Scroll Edge Effect - Soft / Hard component sets in the kit.
scrollEdgeEffect._api: SwiftUI scrollEdgeEffectStyle(_:for:) with .soft or .hard and an edge.

soft._note: Two stacked background blurs: a 10 radius on the container and a 100 radius layer masked by a linear gradient.

uniformToolbar._description: When content scrolls beneath a floating bar, iOS 27 draws a single uniform bar across the top edge instead of letting content show through unevenly. Standard toolbars get this automatically; custom bars tune it through the existing scroll edge effect APIs.
uniformToolbar._trigger: content scrolled under the top bar
uniformToolbar._measured: Modelled on the kit's hard Scroll Edge Effect, which is what a standard toolbar shows once content scrolls under it.

sidebar._ios27Changes: Kit change log 27.0.0: sidebars extended edge to edge; background material updated; sidebar buttons changed to Liquid Glass style with adjusted spacing; selected state updated; symbols tinted.

webApproximation._description: Values the kit does not expose (Figma's GLASS effect hides its blur radius from the REST API). Derived from the native material, not guessed: a SwiftUI .glassEffect() panel was screenshotted over known colour bands on the iOS 26.5 simulator and the black|white boundary profile inside the panel was least-squares fitted to an erf step response. regular -> sigma 5.40pt, clear -> sigma 1.37pt (rmse 0.017/0.021). A control fit outside the panel returns sigma 0.17pt, confirming the method. CSS blur(L) takes L AS the standard deviation (filter-effects-1), so the radii here are sigma / blurScale(0.5) = sigma / 0.9. Large and medium share a value because the kit measures them identical and the native variant covers both.
webApproximation._note: History, so this is not re-litigated: 18/15/9/7 was a guess; briefly raised to 40/32/16/12 on the strength of web reproductions, which was wrong twice over — those reproductions mostly reproduce the CLEAR variant while our default maps to REGULAR, and the sigma-to-CSS conversion was off by 2x (CSS blur(L) is sigma = L, not L/2). Native is far less blurred than either guess.
webApproximation._saturateNote: Apple's material boosts chroma; blur alone renders as a flat wash. Not a plain saturate() natively — solving the native screenshot per band gives ~0.8 on neutral grey, ~1.0 on pure red, ~1.9 on cyan and ~2.4 on magenta, i.e. a chroma-dependent vibrancy a single multiplier cannot express. 1.8 approximates the saturated end, which is where the effect is visible.
webApproximation._alphaNote: The measured bg.a of 0.7 is right FOR CSS. Solving the native screenshot on sRGB codes gives alpha 0.718 / 0.729 / 0.741 per channel, mean 0.729 (the veil is faintly warm); solving in linear light gives 0.49. CSS composites background-color over the backdrop in gamma-encoded sRGB, so the sRGB-code figure is the one that reproduces the native appearance — rgba(255,255,255,0.718) over black yields 183 against the 178 observed. 0.49 would yield 125. The linear-light number describes what the native material does internally and is not the value to ship.
